report.answer_text:
The October 20, 2025 AWS outage was caused by a bug in the automated system that manages DNS for Amazon DynamoDB in AWS’s Northern Virginia region (us-east-1). Two automated updates ran in an unexpected order—a *race condition*—leaving the database service’s regional address with an empty DNS record. Services that depended on that address could no longer connect to DynamoDB. (aws.amazon.com)
The failure then cascaded: AWS had trouble launching new EC2 virtual servers, and some Network Load Balancers had connection failures. Those problems continued for hours after the original DNS issue was fixed. (aws.amazon.com)
Although the fault began in one AWS region, users worldwide saw disruptions. Affected services included Snapchat, Reddit, Signal, Slack, Roblox, Fortnite, and Venmo, as well as Amazon’s own Ring and Alexa. (pbs.org)

quotes.text: The incident was triggered by a latent defect within the service’s automated DNS management system that caused endpoint resolution failures for DynamoDB.

The root cause of this issue was a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS management system that resulted in an incorrect empty DNS record for the service’s regional endpoint (dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) that the automation failed to repair.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes back the core claim that a latent defect or race condition in the automated DynamoDB DNS management system caused the outage, including the us-east-1 endpoint, but they never state the October 20, 2025 date.
pages.page_reason: The page says the October 19–20, 2025 disruption was triggered by a latent defect—a race condition—in DynamoDB’s automated DNS management system in us-east-1.

quotes.text: The root cause of this issue was a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS management system
The timing of these events triggered the latent race condition.
the first Enactor (which had been unusually delayed) applied its much older plan to the regional DDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state that a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS system was the root cause, and that a delayed first Enactor applied an older plan over a newer one, which backs the out-of-order automated updates.
pages.page_reason: The page describes a race condition in which a delayed DNS Enactor applied an older plan after another Enactor had applied a newer plan.

quotes.text: During this period, customers and other AWS services with dependencies on DynamoDB were unable to establish new connections to the service.

When this issue occurred at 11:48 PM PDT, all systems needing to connect to the DynamoDB service in the N. Virginia (us-east-1) Region via the public endpoint immediately began experiencing DNS failures and failed to connect to DynamoDB.
As this plan was deleted, all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state that customers and AWS services dependent on DynamoDB were unable to establish new connections, that systems using the us-east-1 public endpoint failed to connect after DNS failures, and that all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were removed, which together back the claim's main point.
pages.page_reason: The page states that systems needing to connect to DynamoDB in N. Virginia through its public regional endpoint experienced DNS failures and failed to connect.

During this period new instance launches failed with either a “request limit exceeded” or “insufficient capacity” error.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state that after the DynamoDB DNS issue was resolved, customers continued to see increased errors for new instance launches, with launches failing, which backs the claim that AWS had trouble launching new EC2 instances after the DNS failure.
